Step 1: Analyze the problem statement. The problem asks why temperature changes along the coast are usually less extreme (more moderate) than temperature changes farther inland.

Step 2: Consider the physical properties of land and water. Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than land, meaning it takes a lot more energy to heat up or cool down a body of water compared to land. Because of this, the temperature of the ocean remains relatively constant throughout the day and across seasons.

Step 3: Relate the temperature of the ocean to coastal temperatures. Coastal areas are influenced by the air above the ocean (marine effect). Since the ocean's temperature remains fairly constant, it acts as a thermal buffer, moderating the temperatures of the adjacent land and preventing extreme temperature fluctuations. Inland areas lack this large body of water and are therefore subject to more extreme temperature changes.

Step 4: Evaluate the given options:
(A) It is much windier at the coast than farther inland. (Doesn't directly explain temperature moderation)
(B) The temperature of the land remains fairly constant. (False; land heats up and cools down quickly)
(C) It is much less humid at the coast than farther inland. (False; coastal areas are usually more humid)
(D) The temperature of the ocean remains fairly constant. (True; this is the primary reason for coastal temperature moderation)

Final answer: D
